subtitle: For leaders: create shared opportunities for your team to understand and respond across difference, while respecting each person’s individual learning, privacy and actual work duties.
scope: For leaders across DHS. Different points of development describe learning needs explored through an example, not personal orientations inferred from behavior. Advanced describes the complexity of the course application, not a person’s importance or cultural status. No IDI is administered, proprietary activity reproduced or employee result required. Private and practice learning remain available. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: A team can need several kinds of learning at once. One person may be noticing an unfamiliar meaning; another may be reconsidering a familiar assumption; another may want to practice a response. A leader can offer useful choices without diagnosing people or placing them on a cultural ladder. Follow Jules and colleagues through contrasting meanings of responsibility, shared practice and employee-lifecycle situations. The goal is thoughtful leadership that supports personal growth and real work, with privacy and formal responsibilities intact.

intro.heading: Notice learning needs without assigning people a stage
intro.body:
The official IDC describes five orientations: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. The model supports thinking about increasingly complex engagement with difference, but a course exchange does not establish an employee’s orientation. The official IDI has its own qualified assessment and reporting process. Do not infer a personal result from job title, identity, one comment, silence, a quiz answer or a presumed group profile.

In this example, during a DHS learning session, Jules hears different questions. Leah asks why a request for early consultation might be a cultural issue rather than merely a schedule issue. Tom says that people all want to be treated respectfully and wonders what more there is to examine. Riley wants to practice acknowledging another meaning without pretending to agree. Sage prefers to consider the example privately. These are expressed questions and choices, not diagnoses. A single person might raise several of them in another setting.

Jules can respond with support relevant to the activity: clarify a meaning, offer a comparison, rehearse an authentic response or provide private reflection. It is unnecessary to tell Leah which orientation she occupies, call Tom behind or appoint Riley as the team’s culturally advanced expert. Those claims would exceed the evidence and could close down useful learning. Sage’s private choice is not proof of poor engagement.

The course’s Advanced level refers to leading a more complex application with several responsibilities. It does not make its learners more important than others. A meaningful goal is to build shared opportunities and respond to specific questions while retaining everyone’s dignity. The leader can deepen their own understanding too. Use the practice team throughout if considering real colleagues would invite speculation or unnecessary personal recording.

items.title: A question is useful without a label
items.body: Leah’s question gives Jules a way to teach the distinction between practical timing and learned meanings. It does not establish Leah’s whole pattern of engaging difference. Answer the question, invite further inquiry and leave any formal assessment result in its actual process.

items.title: Support can change with the activity
items.body: Riley may want rehearsal now and a basic explanation later. People need not be fixed into beginner, intermediate and advanced groups for every topic. Offer suitable choices for the common purpose and revisit what helps rather than turn an initial response into a permanent learning identity.

items.title: Protect dignity and private choice
items.body: Sage can reflect on the example without sharing a personal story. The choice does not erase a leader’s separate authority for actual work duties, but this course does not turn optional reflection into a performance test. Support growth without requiring cultural disclosure or making a personnel judgment.

tabs.label: Label the speakers
tabs.body: A quick orientation label can appear efficient but replaces a specific question with an unsupported judgment. It may make a colleague defensive or falsely reassuring. Jules can clarify, compare or rehearse without claiming a personal assessment result or distributing employees by presumed cultural rank.

tabs.label: Provide only one response
tabs.body: A long explanation for everyone may overlook Riley’s practice question or Sage’s private path. Shared purpose does not require identical participation. Offer a clear common case with more than one suitable activity, while making the task and any actual work expectations understandable.

tabs.label: Offer relevant support
tabs.body: Jules responds to the expressed questions and keeps a practice private option. The support is specific enough to be useful and flexible enough to change. It preserves the distinction between learning opportunities, actual work evidence and formal assessment rather than assigning status to people.

intro.heading: Make the cultural meaning clear before choosing the support
intro.body:
Jules uses a new practice case about seeking advice on a decision. Avery has learned to express responsibility by bringing an already-developed recommendation to a respected person: preparation shows that the person’s time matters. Remy has learned to express respect by inviting a trusted person into thinking before a recommendation forms: early involvement shows that the relationship and knowledge matter. These meanings developed through important personal and community experiences. They do not describe named groups or establish orientations.

Avery waits to consult, believing that a prepared proposal is considerate. Remy experiences the late invitation as an opportunity to endorse a decision already shaped, rather than share responsibility for its development. Remy’s account does not prove bad intent or require every idea to be discussed immediately. It reveals why the same timing can express respect to one person and exclusion to another. This is the cultural meaning Leah wanted to see; a schedule correction alone would not explain it.

Tom’s observation that everyone wants respect can become a starting point. Jules can affirm the shared value, then ask how each account expresses it and what is missed if a single expression becomes the only standard. Riley can rehearse an honest opening: I wanted to respect your time by preparing first; I understand that an earlier invitation might communicate shared responsibility. Would a discussion while options are still open be useful here? The rehearsal follows a changed perspective and keeps the response subject to the actual situation.

Sage may privately explore why preparation or early consultation feels respectful through the example. That understanding has personal value without a work result. Actual work decisions also have deadlines, delegated authority and consultation requirements; personal meanings do not replace them. Keep those requirements separate and explain the remaining room for a suitable response. The leader’s role is to make inquiry useful, not to certify whose culture is correct.

items.title: Shared respect does not settle expression
items.body: Both Avery and Remy value responsibility and respect. Saying we are all the same can hide the difference in how those values are expressed. Compare the learned meanings so the team can see why intent and experienced participation may differ without inventing a group hierarchy.

items.title: Describe the perspective change
items.body: Avery initially reads early consultation as wasting someone’s time. Remy’s volunteered account offers another meaning: involvement can show trust in shared responsibility. A proposed earlier invitation becomes meaningful when it follows that understanding, rather than when it is merely another calendar entry.

items.title: Keep the actual boundary visible
items.body: An earlier discussion may be possible while options remain open, but a required deadline or authorized decision role still matters. Explain what participation can affect and avoid false promises. Neither personal meaning authorizes an employee to delegate a decision or promise that every suggestion will be adopted.

tabs.label: Use commonality to end inquiry
tabs.body: Affirming respect is valuable, but ending there leaves the contrasting expressions unseen. Remy may continue to experience an endorsement-only invitation while Avery feels misunderstood. Use the shared value to open a comparison instead of treating it as proof that timing has no meaning.

tabs.label: Replace one universal standard with another
tabs.body: Calling early consultation always culturally superior erases contexts where preparation is necessary or welcomed. The example shows individual meanings, not a rule that every person wants the same sequence. Consider the expressed account and actual decision boundaries before proposing a response.

tabs.label: Clarify meanings and choices
tabs.body: Jules helps learners compare preparation-as-care with involvement-as-trust, then explore a suitable invitation. A private interpretation exercise and an optional rehearsal can serve the same understanding. The team can learn without inferring identities, assigning orientations or guaranteeing agreement.

check.feedbackCorrect: The example connects expressed meanings to perspective and behavior while retaining individual scope.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A timing change alone does not establish culturally informed understanding. A shared value can have different expressions. One volunteered account is not a group rule. Teach the contrast and its response implications rather than infer a cultural score or universal preference.

intro.heading: Offer different learning activities without fixing people into tracks
intro.body:
For the Avery and Remy example, Jules can offer three original activities. A meaning comparison helps learners separate observation, familiar interpretation and another expressed meaning. A private reflection invites consideration of why preparation or inclusion may feel respectful. A practice rehearsal tries an authentic invitation while preserving a deadline and decision role. These are course choices, not official IDP exercises or separate ranks assigned to employees.

Leah may begin with the comparison and later try the rehearsal. Riley may discover during rehearsal that the meaning still needs clarification. Tom may privately recognize that a common value does not guarantee a common expression. Sage may use the invented accounts throughout. Choosing one activity does not establish an orientation, and people can change activities without being promoted or demoted. The leader should explain what each option offers rather than decide that some staff are incapable of deeper reflection.

The common purpose is to understand a meaning contrast and consider a suitable response. The activities need enough teaching to serve that purpose. A simple preference survey would not explain why the expressions make sense. An unstructured demand to share cultural stories could pressure disclosure without helping inquiry. A clear practice comparison, an optional question and specific feedback can make the experience engaging while maintaining choice.

Jules can ask whether the activity clarified the question or what remains difficult. Those responses guide another teaching choice; they do not certify cultural competence or provide evidence for a personnel action. Actual assigned work may require a specific product or participation under real agency arrangements, but this course does not establish a new training mandate, accommodation decision or performance rule. Keep optional personal reflection separate and seek the proper process for actual access or work questions.

items.title: Make the options substantive
items.body: A comparison examines learned meanings; reflection deepens self-understanding; rehearsal connects meaning to a response. Explain what each activity helps learners do. items.title: Allow movement without a hierarchy
items.body: Riley can return from rehearsal to comparison when a meaning is unclear. That move is a sensible learning choice, not a demotion. Flexible support lets a person respond to a changing question and prevents the leader from treating an initial activity choice as a stable personal capability.

items.title: Review the support, not private history
items.body: Jules can ask whether a case is clear without requiring a memory, identity or assessment profile. A learner may request another format or use an example privately. Keep actual work or access concerns in their proper processes rather than investigate an employee’s cultural history to explain participation.

tabs.label: Fix employees into permanent tracks
tabs.body: A beginner label based on one question can follow a person across unrelated topics and limit opportunity. It also exceeds the evidence. Offer suitable activity choices for this purpose and revisit them without treating the choice as a permanent personal rank.

tabs.label: Remove teaching in the name of choice
tabs.body: A menu without explanations may leave staff unable to decide what helps. Choice works better when the comparison, reflection and rehearsal each have a clear purpose and useful feedback. Preserve substantial instruction while allowing different ways to engage it.

tabs.label: Use flexible purposeful support
tabs.body: Jules explains the options, retains a private practice route and adjusts support when a question changes. The common purpose stays visible without uniform disclosure or a status hierarchy. Actual assigned work remains separate from any inference about cultural development.

intro.heading: Carry learning through the employee lifecycle
intro.body:
Intercultural leadership can be considered at several points of the employee lifecycle: recruitment and hiring, onboarding, supervision, development and retention. The learning question changes with the situation, but the need to separate meaning, evidence and authority remains. A course does not give a leader permission to replace actual job criteria, alter qualifications or make a personnel decision from a cultural impression.

In a practice hiring preparation case, a panel considers how applicants explain previous work. One participant expects a short individual accomplishment statement. Another applicant’s response begins with the team and context before identifying their own contribution. A learner wonders whether the opening could express respect for shared effort rather than inability to take responsibility. That is a possible meaning to consider, not an identity-based explanation or a verdict about the candidate. The panel still needs evidence related to the actual criterion, asked and evaluated through its authorized consistent process.

In practice onboarding, Jules can explain why questions before an assigned review point matter for the work, rather than assume new staff know what early consultation signifies. In supervision, a leader can examine whether a task-related expectation has been explained and invite a workable response. In development, staff can have access to useful learning opportunities without being excluded by a presumed orientation. Retention questions can examine experience and opportunity through appropriate evidence without claiming that a cultural lesson alone caused a change.

These applications do not require staff to disclose personal results or narrate a background. Leaders can use practice rehearsal to recognize a familiar interpretation and consider another one. The personal insight can matter even if no live hiring or supervisory action follows. For any actual use, retain applicable HR procedures, consistent criteria, information boundaries and delegated authority. A culturally informed question should improve understanding of evidence, not substitute a stereotype or course-created rule for the real decision process.

items.title: Ask for criterion-related evidence
items.body: A contextual opening does not prove either competence or incompetence. In the example, the useful question concerns the person’s actual contribution to the work. Use the authorized consistent approach to obtain and evaluate that evidence rather than reward or penalize a presumed cultural style.

items.title: Explain the work meaning in onboarding
items.body: New staff may not share a supervisor’s interpretation of early questions. Explain the task, review point and reason for raising an unresolved issue. Invite suitable questions without requiring a private history or assuming that a new employee’s silence indicates a cultural deficit.

items.title: Preserve opportunity in development
items.body: An employee should not be excluded from a learning opportunity on the basis of an inferred orientation. This course offers no such personnel rule. Leaders can discuss actual duties and support through their proper processes, while optional cultural reflection remains a legitimate personal learning path.

tabs.label: Use style as a personnel verdict
tabs.body: Equating a contextual opening with poor ownership can obscure criterion-related evidence. Reversing the shortcut and treating the same style as proof of superior teamwork is equally unsupported. Examine the actual contribution through the proper consistent process without inferring identity or cultural status.

tabs.label: Replace requirements with a cultural preference
tabs.body: Understanding a meaning does not authorize a leader to waive a qualification, invent a selection question outside the process or change an assigned role. Actual authority and applicable procedures remain. Separate a thoughtful interpretation from any proposed change that needs the proper decision-maker.

tabs.label: Connect inquiry to real responsibilities
tabs.body: The lifecycle applications help leaders clarify expectations, understand possible meanings and obtain appropriate work evidence. Practice supports that reasoning without a live personnel action. Actual use retains HR roles, consistent criteria, privacy and delegated authority rather than importing an invented course rule.

intro.heading: Keep learning alongside access, privacy and formal duties
intro.body:
A team-learning activity can raise separate access or formal concerns. A leader should recognize those distinctions instead of explain every difficulty as a cultural stage. A learner may prefer fiction because they do not want to disclose personal experience. Someone may also request a disability-related adjustment. Another person may report protected-class harassment or discrimination. These are different matters and should not be folded into an optional development exercise.

In a DHS example, Sage asks for a disability-related adjustment to participate in a learning activity. Under MMB Policy 1433, managers and supervisors must not request medical information or documentation. Any appropriate request for supporting documentation belongs to the ADA Coordinator through the proper process, and the agency policy bars requesting or accepting medical records. Promptly follow the actual request route and identify the authorized decision-maker under the agency’s arrangements. This course does not invent DHS delegations, grant or deny an accommodation or require a diagnosis as the price of a practice option.

In a separate exchange, a learner reports an allegation of protected-class discrimination. MMB Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the affirmative action officer and follow agency procedures. An optional cultural dialogue is not an investigation, finding or substitute for that reporting. Preserve any assigned formal role rather than improvise private handling outside actual authority.

Jules can still make the practice materials understandable and allow private reflection. Such teaching support does not promise a formal accommodation outcome or erase actual task requirements. Keep personal accounts and any actual confidential records within their proper boundaries. A leader can learn more about their own assumptions concerning help and participation without demanding another person’s diagnosis, profile or history. Personal growth and operational duties can coexist when neither is treated as a replacement for the other.

items.title: Separate ordinary choice from a formal request
items.body: A practice option can be available to everyone without asking why a person chooses it. When a disability-related request is made, follow the actual accommodation process rather than treat the learning menu as a complete response. Do not grant or deny the request from a course or invent an agency decision role.

items.title: Keep documentation in the proper role
items.body: MMB Policy 1433 prohibits manager and supervisor requests for medical information or documentation, not just complete records. The ADA Coordinator handles appropriate documentation questions through the formal process. A leader should not gather diagnosis details into a learning note, and medical records must not be requested or accepted.

items.title: Report without postponing for dialogue
items.body: Under MMB Policy 1436, immediate manager and supervisor reporting belongs with HR or the affirmative action officer and agency procedures. A respectful conversation cannot be made a prerequisite. Continue appropriate learning separately without deciding an allegation privately or overriding assigned formal responsibilities.

tabs.label: Explain every concern as development
tabs.body: An access request or allegation can be mishandled if treated as evidence that a person needs a different cultural stage. The explanation is unsupported and can delay the proper route. Recognize the actual concern, preserve privacy and use the assigned process without an orientation label.

tabs.label: Collect private details to tailor learning
tabs.body: A leader does not need diagnosis or an individual profile to offer examples and clear teaching. Medical information and documentation requests are prohibited for managers and supervisors under Policy 1433. Keep necessary formal questions in their proper role rather than assemble a cultural or medical learning file.

tabs.label: Offer support and preserve the formal route
tabs.body: Jules provides suitable practice learning choices while promptly following actual access and reporting responsibilities. The leader does not promise a formal outcome or substitute a dialogue for required handling. This keeps personal growth, participation and agency duties connected without collapsing their roles.

Private growth can matter without a team metric.
lessons.statement: Review what the opportunity supported, not who is culturally ahead.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Review the learning environment without ranking the team
intro.body:
Jules can review the learning opportunity by asking what the example clarified and what support would help next. Leah now distinguishes a schedule issue from a learned meaning of respect. Tom recognizes that a shared value can have different expressions. Riley finds the rehearsal useful but wants another example. Sage offers no personal account and privately retains a question about help. These are bounded learning experiences, not a ranking of the colleagues.

Separate kinds of evidence. Attendance records show participation, not cultural competence. A volunteered perspective gain shows what that learner chooses to express, not a permanent orientation. Rehearsing an invitation is practice, not proof that an actual relationship improved. If the team later makes a work change, any effect claim needs suitable evidence and its own responsibilities. Do not say there are no barriers simply because no one disclosed a difficulty. Unknown information should remain unknown.

The official IDI has a formal group report process. Any actual group assessment should remain within its qualified process and information arrangements; a group summary cannot be used to infer each individual result or demand private profiles from members. This course supplies neither a group score nor a home-made substitute. Course answers, demographic assumptions and learning choices should not be aggregated into employee orientation labels.

Jules can revise the shared opportunity: explain the meaning comparison more clearly, provide another practice rehearsal or preserve more private reflection space. Small-team feedback should be proportionate and appropriately handled; the course does not require collecting identity-linked accounts or measuring each person’s cultural stage. Personal insight has value on its own. You can keep it private. The leader’s own understanding can also deepen. Choose the next support because it helps the purpose, not because it creates a more advanced-looking team or a favorable dashboard.

inThisLesson: Distinguish participation, perspective gain, response practice and actual work effects.
Choose proportionate feedback about the learning environment without collecting personal profiles.
Revise the shared learning opportunity while recognizing private growth.
Which report is defensible?
lessons.keyStatement: Review what the opportunity supported, not who is culturally ahead.

items.title: Keep the evidence categories honest
items.body: Leah’s clarification, Riley’s practice request and an attendance count are different facts. None establishes an individual orientation or a work effect. Name the supported claim and its limits before deciding what teaching to revise; missing disclosure is not evidence that everyone found the experience accessible or useful.

items.title: Preserve formal assessment boundaries
items.body: A real group IDI report belongs to its actual qualified process. It cannot be read as the personal result of every member, and this course does not construct an equivalent from answers or identities. Keep the learning review focused on the opportunity and expressed questions rather than demand private assessment details.

items.title: Revise for useful learning
items.body: Another practice case can meet a remaining question without naming a deficient colleague. Private growth can remain unseen and legitimate. The review can improve clarity, support and opportunity while leaving actual work effects for their own evidence and avoiding a ranking of cultural worth.

tabs.label: Build a home-made stage dashboard
tabs.body: Combining quiz answers, participation and presumed identities into a stage score exceeds the evidence and creates a false assessment. A formal group process is separate. Review what the learning opportunity supported without constructing individual orientation labels or personnel rankings.

tabs.label: Treat silence as full success
tabs.body: No disclosed concern may reflect privacy, uncertainty or many other circumstances. It does not establish a barrier-free experience or universal benefit. Provide a proportionate way to request support, keep unknowns open and recognize that private understanding can remain unreported.

tabs.label: Review the opportunity and continue
tabs.body: Jules uses expressed questions to improve teaching, separates practice from work effects and preserves private learning. This supports a continuing shared purpose without compulsory profiles or a cultural hierarchy. The next activity responds to a question rather than a desire for a favorable score.

check.question: Which review statement is most accurate?
check.correct: The team’s expressed questions guide further support; attendance, private growth, practice and actual work effects remain distinct and do not establish personal orientations.
wrong: High attendance proves every colleague’s intercultural competence.
No disclosed concerns proves the session had no barriers.
A group profile establishes the individual result of every member.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review preserves the limits of each kind of information and focuses on useful learning support.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance cannot establish competence. Silence cannot prove that no barriers exist. A group summary cannot be substituted for every individual result. Recognize supported learning, keep unknowns open and revise the opportunity without ranking people.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The practice session has high attendance and few public comments. Jules wants to report its value.
options: Describe participation and the bounded expressed feedback, leave unreported experiences unknown and choose further support without a competence score.
Report that every employee has reached a higher orientation.
Declare that there were no barriers because none were publicly disclosed.
responses: This preserves actual information and meaningful next steps.
The course supplies no individual assessment or score change.
Silence is not proof that no barrier existed.

lessons.transfer: Privately examine the practice review and choose a useful next support. Do not collect real colleagues’ private profiles or cultural rankings.

move.control: You can review the opportunity and your own understanding without a personal hierarchy.
move.failure: Participation or missing feedback is turned into an invented assessment or reassuring result.
move.next: State the supported learning information, retain uncertainty and choose another suitable support.

jobAid.subtitle: Lead a shared learning opportunity with different suitable paths.
remember: Respond to expressed questions; do not infer an individual IDC orientation from behavior, identity, course answers or a group summary.
Advanced concerns application complexity, not a person’s importance or cultural status.
Private and practice understanding matter without compulsory disclosure, a work metric or a personnel judgment.

sections.heading: Support understanding and practice
items: Name the shared purpose and make the learned meaning contrast clear.
Offer substantial comparison, private reflection and practice rehearsal as suitable choices, not fixed personal tracks.
Connect a response to the perspective gained while retaining honesty, choice and actual decision boundaries.
Use employee-lifecycle examples to clarify work and opportunity without replacing consistent criteria, HR processes or delegated authority.

sections.heading: Preserve duties and review honestly
items: Follow actual accommodation routes; managers and supervisors must not request medical information or documentation, and medical records must not be requested or accepted.
Immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents through HR or the affirmative action officer and agency procedures; optional learning is not a substitute.
Keep participation, learning insight, practice and any actual work effect as distinct claims, leaving missing information unknown.
Revise the learning opportunity from proportionate feedback; formal IDI profiles and qualified processes remain separate.

sources.title: IDI: Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Describes the official five orientations and the perspective-and-behavior meaning of Adaptation. Learning questions do not establish a colleague’s orientation; Advanced is a program course level.

sources.title: IDI: Assessment and reports
sources.note: Public distinction between group reports, confidential individual profiles and customized assessment-based development plans. No report, assessment item or proprietary activity is reproduced; a group summary is not substituted for an individual result.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Conceptual discussion of experience, comparison, reflection and personal growth. The flexible activities and employee-lifecycle examples are newly authored, not copied source exercises or new Minnesota personnel requirements.

sources.title: MMB: Assessing and setting qualifications
sources.note: State guidance addresses job-related qualifications, selection and assessment. The course example retains established criteria, consistent procedures and responsible authority rather than creating a cultural hiring rule.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: Reasonable accommodation
sources.note: Direct Minnesota policy for prompt request routing, actual decision authority and the prohibition on manager/supervisor medical information or documentation requests. Appropriate documentation belongs with the ADA Coordinator; medical records must not be requested or accepted.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Direct Minnesota policy for immediate manager and supervisor reporting to HR or the affirmative action officer and agency procedures, preserving assigned formal roles. Learning is not an investigation or required reporting substitute.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency context for equity in actual work. Optional course practice does not replace applicable formal analysis, tools, required training or authorized decisions.
